content: 1. Strengthening reporting and monitoring systems for immunization programs is essential to improve the quality of data on birth dose vaccinations. The birth dose should be followed by two or three additional doses to complete the primary vaccination series. 2. Women co-infected with HIV and HBV should receive tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF)-based antiretroviral therapy (ART) to prevent mother-to-child transmission of HBV. This is in addition to the three-dose HBV vaccination for all infants, including a timely birth dose. 3. For individuals with HIV and uncomplicated Plasmodium falciparum malaria, avoid using artesunate + sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine if they are on co-trimoxazole, and avoid artesunate + amodiaquine if they are on efavirenz or zidovudine. 4. In Eastern Africa, people co-infected with visceral leishmaniasis and HIV should be treated with liposomal amphotericin B (up to a total of 30 mg/kg administered on days 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, and 11) combined with miltefosine (100 mg/day for 28 days). In South-East Asia, the same regimen is recommended, but miltefosine is administered for 14 days. Secondary prophylaxis should be provided after the first episode of visceral leishmaniasis for all co-infected individuals. 5. For women living with HIV, the WHO recommends using HPV DNA detection as the primary screening test for cervical cancer, rather than visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA) or cytology. Existing programs using quality-assured cytology should continue until HPV DNA testing becomes operational. Programs using VIA should transition rapidly due to challenges with quality assurance. 6. HPV DNA primary screening tests with triage are preferred over those without triage for cervical cancer prevention in women living with HIV. Triage options include partial genotyping, colposcopy, VIA, or cytology. The choice of triage method depends on feasibility, training, program quality assurance, and available resources. 7. Regular cervical cancer screening should begin at age 25 for women living with HIV. Screening intervals of 3–5 years are recommended when using HPV DNA testing. If HPV DNA testing is unavailable, VIA or cytology should be used every three years. Screening can stop after age 50 if two consecutive negative results are obtained. 8. Women living with HIV who test positive on an HPV DNA screening test but negative on a triage test should be retested with HPV DNA testing in 12 months. If negative, they can move to the recommended screening interval. Similarly, women with positive cytology results but normal colposcopy findings should follow the same retesting protocol. 9. Women treated for histologically confirmed CIN 2/3, adenocarcinoma in situ, or due to a positive screening test should be retested with HPV DNA testing at 12 months. If negative, they should be retested again at 12 months and, if negative again, move to the recommended screening interval. 10. For women with adenocarcinoma in situ, large loop excision of the transformation zone or cold-knife conization is recommended. Loop excision may be preferred for women of reproductive age, while cold-knife conization is preferred when margin interpretation of the histological specimen is critical. 11. Cardiovascular disease screening in low-resource settings should target individuals over 40 years old, smokers, those with known hypertension or diabetes, individuals with high waist circumference, and those with a family history of diabetes or premature cardiovascular disease. Prevention strategies should address modifiable risk factors such as blood pressure, smoking, obesity, unhealthy diet, and physical inactivity. 12. Depression assessment and management should be included in HIV care services for all individuals living with HIV. 13. Men who have sex with men (MSM) and transgender individuals with symptomatic sexually transmitted infections (STIs) should receive syndromic management and treatment. Periodic testing for asymptomatic urethral and rectal N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis infections using nucleic acid amplification tests (NAAT) is suggested. Serological testing for asymptomatic syphilis is strongly recommended. 14. Female sex workers in lowand middle-income countries should be offered periodic screening for asymptomatic STIs. All pregnant women should be screened for syphilis during their first antenatal care visit, regardless of the prevalence of syphilis in the setting. 15. For individuals presenting with urethral discharge, management should be based on quality-assured molecular assays. In settings without molecular testing, syndromic treatment should be provided to ensure same-day treatment. 16. For individuals presenting with vaginal discharge, treatment for N. gonorrhoeae, C. trachomatis, and/or T. vaginalis should be provided during the same visit. If molecular assays are unavailable, treatment should be based on rapid point-of-care tests or syndromic management. Bacterial vaginosis and candidiasis should be treated based on clinical presentation or microscopy results, if available. 17. Sexually active women with lower abdominal pain should be assessed for pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) and treated syndromically during the same visit. Testing for N. gonorrhoeae, C. trachomatis, and Mycoplasma genitalium should be conducted if available to support partner management. 18. For individuals with genital ulcers, including anorectal ulcers, treatment should be based on quality-assured molecular assays. In settings without molecular testing, syndromic treatment should be provided to ensure same-day treatment. 19. For individuals with anorectal discharge who report receptive anal sex, management should be based on molecular assay results. In settings without molecular testing, syndromic treatment should be provided. 20. Good clinical practice for men includes taking a detailed medical and sexual history, assessing STI risk, performing a physical examination of the genital and anal areas, offering HIV and syphilis testing, and ensuring partner notification and treatment history are reviewed for persistent symptoms. 21. Good clinical practice for women includes taking a medical and sexual history, performing abdominal and pelvic examinations to assess for PID, pregnancy, or surgical conditions, and conducting external vulvo-vaginal examinations to identify lesions, discharge, or erythema. Bimanual examinations should assess for cervical motion tenderness and the presence and characteristics of vaginal discharge. Persistent or recurrent vaginal discharge should prompt referral to a laboratory-equipped center for diagnosis and antimicrobial resistance testing.
